To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the growth in global agricultural output in the past decade was driven by increases in TFP; (2) TFP growth was not associated with lower land conversion in most of the world; (3) the expansion of cropland in response to increases in productivity was more than offset globally by indirect land use changes, and (4) the expansion of global cropland would have been much larger if it had not been for increases in TFP.

the introduction of technologies with the potential to improve agricultural productivity is likely to lead to land expansion, which, however, is offset by indirect land effects, and that the indirect effects are likely to be more important than the direct effects.

1) TFP growth has contributed to a more sustainable global food system in terms of lower land expansion pressures, but only in the decade of the 2000's, and 2) TFP growth will need to accelerate in the next 15 years to prevent land expansion, which is the main driver of land-use change emissions, in the face of projected increases in global population and income per capita.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extent to which TFP growth is associated with a more sustainable food supply.
the sustainability of agricultural TFP growth, and its implications for the sustainability of farming in general.
the question of whether the growth in agricultural productivity that we have experienced during the last decades has been a boon for the sustainability of our food system, as it is often assumed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the absence of TTP growth, land expansion would have been larger, but that the observed expansion is less harmful than what would have been the case in the absence of productivity growth.
TFP growth has been associated with lower land use emissions and lower land expansion pressures, but that such effects are more than compensated by indirect land use changes.

the growth in agricultural TFP in the last thirty or so years has contributed to a more sustainable farming system, in the sense of reducing the pressure of cropland expansion on the world's natural resources.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the absence of TFD growth, global croplands would have expanded by $\approx$ 100 Mha during 2001–2010, with $\approx$ 50 Mha in the four most biodiversity-rich biomes, and that current rates of growth are insufficient to reverse this trend during the next decade.

, in spite of the fact that the growth in agricultural productivity has been accompanied by land contraction during 2001 to 2010, such contraction is insufficient to prevent further expansion of croplands, which would have occurred in the absence of such productivity growth.

, although the observed TFP growth has been associated with lower emissions and lower land expansion, the current pace of TFP growth is insufficient to prevent further expansion of croplands in most of the world.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sustainability of agricultural intensification hinges critically on how the productivity growth is achieved, with the indirect effects of land expansion being a key factor.
, despite the recent slowdown in land expansion in most regions of interest, the sustainability of the current food production regime is far from assured.

, in the absence of a global agreement on how to share land expansion costs, the current rate of TFP growth is insufficient to avoid further land expansion in many countries, with the attendant environmental and social consequences.
